title: Oil Drops Over $2 as Iran-Oman Talks Revive Hopes for Strait of Hormuz Reopening
excerpt: Brent crude falls to a two-week low after the two countries discuss a temporary navigational corridor and mine clearance in the vital waterway.
body:
• Brent crude fell $2.73 (3.08%) to $85.85 per barrel, while WTI dropped $2.21 (2.68%) to $80.15 — both hitting two-week lows.
  • Iran and Oman discussed a “joint temporary navigational corridor” through the Strait of Hormuz and agreed to clear the waterway of mines.
  • The strait carried roughly 20% of global oil and LNG shipments before the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran began in February 2026.

Oil prices fell more than $2 a barrel on Wednesday, hitting their lowest levels since August 10, after talks between Iran and Oman revived market hopes that the Strait of Hormuz could partially reopen and ease shipping constraints that have disrupted Middle East energy flows for nearly six months.

Brent crude futures dropped $2.73, or 3.08%, to $85.85 a barrel by midday GMT. West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell $2.21, or 2.68%, to $80.15.

The Corridor Proposal

Iran and Oman announced on Tuesday that they had discussed establishing “a joint temporary navigational corridor” through the strait and agreed to clear it of mines — the most concrete progress toward restoring traffic since the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran began in late February.

The Strait of Hormuz, situated between Iran and Oman, carried approximately one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the conflict. Traffic through the waterway has plummeted, with Persian Gulf flows running at roughly 36% of pre-war levels in recent weeks, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

“The market has moved from pricing a high probability of prolonged disruption and renewed escalation towards pricing partial reopening, negotiated shipping arrangements and a lower risk of renewed military confrontation.”

— Ole Hansen, Head of Commodity Strategy, Saxo Bank

Cautious Optimism

Analysts cautioned that significant obstacles remain. Iran has previously sought fees of 5% to 7% on cargo values for ships transiting the strait, while Oman has proposed around 3%. Washington wants no fees at all. U.S. sanctions and restrictive insurance clauses complicate any payment mechanism.

“It’s renewed focus on the discussion between Iran and Oman regarding a deal for transiting oil and other petrochemicals through the Strait of Hormuz. So that sort of creates some optimism,” said Bjarne Schieldrop, chief commodities analyst at SEB Research.

The talks follow a volatile period for oil markets. Prices swung sharply last week — dropping over 7% on deal hopes before rebounding 5% after Iran issued additional conditions, including demands that the U.S. lift sanctions and pay compensation.

Wider Market Implications

A credible reopening agreement would remove a substantial geopolitical risk premium from oil prices. Goldman Sachs estimates that Brent is fairly valued at around $80 per barrel based on inventory fundamentals, suggesting current prices still carry a modest premium tied to Hormuz uncertainty.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Wednesday that Iran and Oman have reached agreement on their share of the strait and its revenues, but the waterway will not reopen if the U.S. does not accept their conditions.

The on-again, off-again nature of the negotiations has conditioned traders to wait for tangible evidence — verified tanker movements or formal multilateral agreements — before fully unwinding risk positions. For now, the market is pricing cautious optimism, but a final resolution remains elusive.
nri_angle: Lower oil prices would ease fuel and transportation costs globally, while a Hormuz reopening could stabilize energy markets that affect inflation in the US and India.
